claim: Mitochondria play a central role in metabolic homeostasis.
source: Mitochondria play a central role in metabolic homeostasis, and dysfunction of this organelle underpins the etiology of many heritable and aging-related diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Dysfunction of mitochondria underpins the etiology of many heritable and aging-related diseases.
source: Mitochondria play a central role in metabolic homeostasis, and dysfunction of this organelle underpins the etiology of many heritable and aging-related diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial dysfunction and disease.

claim: Tetrapeptides with alternating cationic and aromatic residues such as SS-31 (elamipretide) show promise as therapeutic compounds for mitochondrial disorders.
source: Tetrapeptides with alternating cationic and aromatic residues such as SS-31 (elamipretide) show promise as therapeutic compounds for mitochondrial disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on SS-31 efficacy.

claim: This study presents the first structural models for this class of compounds.
source: We present the first structural models for this class of compounds, obtained with Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and molecular dynamics approaches, showing that all analogs except for SS-31 form compact reverse turn conformations in the membrane-bound state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on NMR and MD data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All analogs except for SS-31 form compact reverse turn conformations in the membrane-bound state.
source: We present the first structural models for this class of compounds, obtained with Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and molecular dynamics approaches, showing that all analogs except for SS-31 form compact reverse turn conformations in the membrane-bound state.
evidence: This is supported by NMR and MD data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All peptide analogs bound cardiolipin-containing membranes.
source: All peptide analogs bound cardiolipin-containing membranes, yet they had significant differences in equilibrium binding behavior and membrane interactions.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Peptide analogs had significant differences in equilibrium binding behavior and membrane interactions.
source: All peptide analogs bound cardiolipin-containing membranes, yet they had significant differences in equilibrium binding behavior and membrane interactions.
evidence: This is supported by ITC and other biophysical data in Figures 2-5.

claim: Analogs had markedly different effects on membrane surface charge.
source: Notably, analogs had markedly different effects on membrane surface charge, supporting a mechanism in which modulation of membrane electrostatics is a key feature of their mechanism of action.
evidence: This is supported by ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Modulation of membrane electrostatics is a key feature of the mechanism of action of these peptides.
source: Notably, analogs had markedly different effects on membrane surface charge, supporting a mechanism in which modulation of membrane electrostatics is a key feature of their mechanism of action.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed effects on membrane surface charge.

claim: The peptides had no strict requirement for side chain composition or sequence register to permeate cells and target mitochondria in mammalian cell culture assays.
source: The peptides had no strict requirement for side chain composition or sequence register to permeate cells and target mitochondria in mammalian cell culture assays.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All four peptides were pharmacologically active in serum withdrawal cell stress models.
source: All four peptides were pharmacologically active in serum withdrawal cell stress models yet showed significant differences in their abilities to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, preserve ATP content, and promote cell survival.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The four peptides showed significant differences in their abilities to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, preserve ATP content, and promote cell survival.
source: All four peptides were pharmacologically active in serum withdrawal cell stress models yet showed significant differences in their abilities to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, preserve ATP content, and promote cell survival.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The analog containing tryptophan side chains, SPN10, had the strongest impact on most membrane properties.
source: Within our peptide set, the analog containing tryptophan side chains, SPN10, had the strongest impact on most membrane properties and showed greatest efficacy in cell culture studies.
evidence: This is supported by biophysical and cell culture data in Figures 2-6.

claim: SPN10 showed greatest efficacy in cell culture studies.
source: Within our peptide set, the analog containing tryptophan side chains, SPN10, had the strongest impact on most membrane properties and showed greatest efficacy in cell culture studies.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Side chain composition and register influence the activity of these mitochondria-targeted peptides.
source: Taken together, these results show that side chain composition and register influence the activity of these mitochondria-targeted peptides, helping provide a framework for the rational design of next-generation therapeutics with enhanced potency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of the four peptide analogs.

claim: Mitochondria house the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes that produce >90% of cellular ATP.
source: As regulators of energy metabolism, mitochondria house the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes that produce >90% of cellular ATP.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria coordinate key cellular processes including lipid biosynthesis, ion homeostasis, and cell death.
source: Mitochondria also coordinate key cellular processes including lipid biosynthesis, ion homeostasis, and cell death.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is central to the etiology of many complex pathologies including cancer, cardiopathy, neurodegeneration, aging-related ailments, and heritable (primary) mitochondrial disease.
source: Consequently, mitochondrial dysfunction, particularly in tissues with high energy demand, is central to the etiology of many complex pathologies including cancer, cardiopathy, neurodegeneration, aging-related ailments, and heritable (primary) mitochondrial disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial dysfunction and disease.

claim: There are currently no FDA-approved therapeutics for the treatment of mitochondrial diseases.
source: Despite this, there are currently no FDA-approved therapeutics for the treatment of mitochondrial diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the current state of therapeutics.

claim: Mitochondria-targeted cationic-aromatic tetrapeptides are among the most promising pharmacological interventions under development for the treatment of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Mitochondria-targeted cationic-aromatic tetrapeptides are among the most promising pharmacological interventions under development for the treatment of mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on these peptides.

claim: SS peptides are synthetic C-terminally amidated tetrapeptides with a motif of alternating cationic and aromatic residues.
source: Also termed Szeto-Schiller (SS) peptides, these first-in-class compounds are synthetic C-terminally amidated tetrapeptides with a motif of alternating cationic and aromatic residues that is thought to be important for their ability to traverse membranes in a variety of cell types and to concentrate in mitochondria (Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the peptides supported by citations.

claim: The alternating cationic and aromatic residue motif is thought to be important for the ability of SS peptides to traverse membranes in a variety of cell types and to concentrate in mitochondria.
source: Also termed Szeto-Schiller (SS) peptides, these first-in-class compounds are synthetic C-terminally amidated tetrapeptides with a motif of alternating cationic and aromatic residues that is thought to be important for their ability to traverse membranes in a variety of cell types and to concentrate in mitochondria (Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS-31 improves electron transfer efficiency and increases ATP production while reducing electron leak and reactive oxygen species production in isolated mitochondria and cell cultures.
source: Studies with isolated mitochondria and cell cultures show that SS-31 improves electron transfer efficiency and increases ATP production while reducing electron leak and reactive oxygen species production (Zhao et al., 2004; Birk et al., 2014; Birk et al., 2013; Siegel et al., 2013; Anderson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS-31 maintains cellular bioenergetics under stress conditions such as ischemia, hypoxia, and aging-related dysfunction in animal studies.
source: Animal studies have demonstrated the ability of SS-31 to maintain cellular bioenergetics under stress conditions such as ischemia, hypoxia, and aging-related dysfunction (Allen et al., 2020; Campbell et al., 2019; Szeto, 2018; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The clinical efficacy of SS-31 has been demonstrated for primary mitochondrial disorders.
source: The clinical efficacy of SS-31 has been demonstrated for primary mitochondrial disorders (Zhao et al., 2017; Reid Thompson et al., 2021) and for age-related chronic diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Roshanravan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The clinical efficacy of SS-31 has been demonstrated for age-related chronic diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The clinical efficacy of SS-31 has been demonstrated for primary mitochondrial disorders (Zhao et al., 2017; Reid Thompson et al., 2021) and for age-related chronic diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Roshanravan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS peptides target the lipid bilayers of mitochondrial membranes through interactions with cardiolipin (CL).
source: Early studies suggested that SS peptides target the lipid bilayers of mitochondrial membranes through interactions with cardiolipin (CL) (Birk et al., 2014; Birk et al., 2013; Birk et al., 2015), the anionic phospholipid that is enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) and required for proper membrane morphology and function of membrane-bound complexes (Paradies et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cardiolipin is the anionic phospholipid that is enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) and required for proper membrane morphology and function of membrane-bound complexes.
source: Early studies suggested that SS peptides target the lipid bilayers of mitochondrial membranes through interactions with cardiolipin (CL) (Birk et al., 2014; Birk et al., 2013; Birk et al., 2015), the anionic phospholipid that is enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) and required for proper membrane morphology and function of membrane-bound complexes (Paradies et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SS-31 inhibited peroxidase activity of cytochrome c in model systems.
source: This bilayer-mediated mechanism is supported by work with model systems in which peptide inhibited peroxidase activity of cytochrome c (Birk et al., 2014) and improved cristae ultrastructure (Szeto and Liu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS-31 improved cristae ultrastructure in model systems.
source: This bilayer-mediated mechanism is supported by work with model systems in which peptide inhibited peroxidase activity of cytochrome c (Birk et al., 2014) and improved cristae ultrastructure (Szeto and Liu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS-31 affected lamellar bilayer properties including lipid lateral diffusion and packing interactions.
source: Recent work from our group quantitatively evaluated SS-31 interactions with CL-containing membranes, showing that the peptide affected lamellar bilayer properties (e.g. lipid lateral diffusion and packing interactions), with the most notable effect being on membrane electrostatics based on down-regulation of the surface potential (ψs) that originates from the negatively-charged membrane interface (Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The most notable effect of SS-31 on CL-containing membranes was on membrane electrostatics based on down-regulation of the surface potential (ψs).
source: Recent work from our group quantitatively evaluated SS-31 interactions with CL-containing membranes, showing that the peptide affected lamellar bilayer properties (e.g. lipid lateral diffusion and packing interactions), with the most notable effect being on membrane electrostatics based on down-regulation of the surface potential (ψs) that originates from the negatively-charged membrane interface (Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The SS-31 interactome includes a subset of membrane complexes primarily involved in ATP-generating processes.
source: Based on a crosslinking/mass-spectrometry approach with a biotinylated SS-31 analog, the SS-31 interactome was shown to include a subset of membrane complexes primarily involved in ATP-generating processes (Chavez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In aged cardiomyocytes, SS-31 reduced proton leak mediated by the adenosine nucleotide transporter (ANT1) and stabilized the ATP synthasome.
source: Moreover, in aged cardiomyocytes, SS-31 was shown to reduce proton leak mediated by the adenosine nucleotide transporter (ANT1) and stabilize the ATP synthasome (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Almost all of the SS-31-interactive proteins are known to bind CL.
source: Notably, almost all of these SS-31-interactive proteins are known to themselves bind CL.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge of protein-lipid interactions.

claim: Mitochondrial lipid composition plays a key role in modulating the molecular interactions of SS-31.
source: Therefore, mitochondrial lipid composition plays a key role in modulating the molecular interactions of SS-31.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SS-31-interactive proteins bind CL.

claim: The lack of information relating the structure and function of these mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptides presents a barrier to a full understanding of their mechanism of action.
source: Despite these insights, the lack of information relating the structure and function of these mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptides presents a barrier to a full understanding of their MoA.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Three sequence-variant peptides were evaluated that differed with respect to aromatic side chain content and cationic/aromatic register, compared with the SS-31 benchmark.
source: In this study, we evaluated three sequence-variant peptides that differed with respect to aromatic side chain content and cationic/aromatic register, compared with the SS-31 benchmark.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: The test set included two analogs with B-φ-B-φ register, SS-31 and SPN4.
source: Our test set (Figure 1A) included two analogs with B-φ-B-φ register, SS-31 (our benchmark), and SPN4.
evidence: This is a description of the peptide test set shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SS-31 and SPN4 differ only with respect to the second-position aromatic residue.
source: These two analogs differ only with respect to the second-position aromatic residue.
evidence: This is a description of the peptide sequences shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SS-31 contains the unnatural amino acid 2,6-dimethyl tyrosine (Dmt).
source: SS-31 contains the unnatural amino acid 2,6-dimethyl tyrosine (Dmt), known to be important for free radical scavenging by this peptide (Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the SS-31 sequence shown in Figure 1A, supported by citations.

claim: 2,6-dimethyl tyrosine (Dmt) is known to be important for free radical scavenging by SS-31.
source: SS-31 contains the unnatural amino acid 2,6-dimethyl tyrosine (Dmt), known to be important for free radical scavenging by this peptide (Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPN4 replaces Dmt with Tyr.
source: By contrast, SPN4 replaces Dmt with Tyr.
evidence: This is a description of the SPN4 sequence shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The test set included two analogs with φ-B-φ-B register, SS-20 and SPN10.
source: Additionally, our test set included two analogs with φ-B-φ-B register, SS-20, and SPN10.
evidence: This is a description of the peptide test set shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SS-20 does not possess the free radical scavenging properties of SS-31.
source: With its Phe/Phe aromatic composition, SS-20 does not possess the free radical scavenging properties of SS-31; however, SS-20 is known to target mitochondria (Liu et al., 2018; Alta et al., 2017) and has also demonstrated efficacy with many mitochondrial disease models (Cho et al., 2007; Szeto et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenolic OH groups in SS-20, supported by citations.

claim: SS-20 is known to target mitochondria.
source: With its Phe/Phe aromatic composition, SS-20 does not possess the free radical scavenging properties of SS-31; however, SS-20 is known to target mitochondria (Liu et al., 2018; Alta et al., 2017) and has also demonstrated efficacy with many mitochondrial disease models (Cho et al., 2007; Szeto et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SS-20 has demonstrated efficacy with many mitochondrial disease models.
source: With its Phe/Phe aromatic composition, SS-20 does not possess the free radical scavenging properties of SS-31; however, SS-20 is known to target mitochondria (Liu et al., 2018; Alta et al., 2017) and has also demonstrated efficacy with many mitochondrial disease models (Cho et al., 2007; Szeto et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Scavenging activity is not an essential feature of the mechanism of action of this class of compounds.
source: This confirms that scavenging activity is not an essential feature of the MoA of this class of compounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the efficacy of SS-20, which lacks scavenging activity.

claim: SPN10 is unique in the test set in that it contains only L-enantiomer side chains.
source: Finally, SPN10 is unique in our test set in that it contains only L-enantiomer side chains, and it has two Trp residues that combine a bulky bicyclic indole group with a pyrrole-like NH that can mediate H-bond interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the SPN10 sequence shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SPN10 has two Trp residues that combine a bulky bicyclic indole group with a pyrrole-like NH that can mediate H-bond interactions.
source: Finally, SPN10 is unique in our test set in that it contains only L-enantiomer side chains, and it has two Trp residues that combine a bulky bicyclic indole group with a pyrrole-like NH that can mediate H-bond interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the SPN10 sequence shown in Figure 1A, based on chemical knowledge.

claim: The free peptides are extended but have some residual structure due to aromatic interactions.
source: The free peptides are extended but have some residual structure due to aromatic interactions
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Small water-soluble and membrane-active peptides are typically disordered in solution and adopt their bioactive conformations only upon binding membranes.
source: Small water-soluble and membrane-active peptides are typically disordered in solution and adopt their bioactive conformations only upon binding membranes (Avci et al., 2018; Kabelka and Vácha, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Even very short peptides can have preferred conformations in aqueous solution, particularly if they are enriched in aromatic residues.
source: However, even very short peptides can have preferred conformations in aqueous solution (Jas et al., 2019), particularly if they are enriched in aromatic residues.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The NMR structures of peptides in solution are relatively disordered extended conformations.
source: The NMR structures of peptides in solution are relatively disordered extended conformations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NMR assignments show few, if any, nuclear Overhauser effects (NOEs) for the peptides in solution.
source: NMR assignments (see Supplementary file 1) show few, if any, nuclear Overhauser effects (NOEs) (shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panel A), which is consistent with their molecular masses of ~600 Da, as this is near the zero-crossing point for the NOE (Williamson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The molecular masses of the peptides are ~600 Da, which is near the zero-crossing point for the NOE.
source: NMR assignments (see Supplementary file 1) show few, if any, nuclear Overhauser effects (NOEs) (shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panel A), which is consistent with their molecular masses of ~600 Da, as this is near the zero-crossing point for the NOE (Williamson, 2009).
evidence: This is based on the peptide sequences and a citation to NMR theory.

claim: SS-20 is in a monomeric state under the conditions used for NMR analysis.
source: Furthermore, using SS-20 as a representative peptide, we used pulse field gradient (PFG) NMR diffusion experiments (Whitehead et al., 2022) to confirm that the free peptides are in a monomeric state under the conditions used for NMR analysis (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by PFG-NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ROESY data were collected to characterize distance contacts in solution.
source: To characterize distance contacts in solution, we therefore collected rotating frame nuclear Overhauser effect spectroscopy (ROESY) data (Williamson, 2009), as the signs of crosspeaks in this experiment are invariant to molecular size (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panel B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Roughly 30–50 distance constraints per peptide were obtained for NMR structure calculations.
source: We obtained roughly 30–50 distance constraints per peptide for NMR structure calculations (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the NMR data used for structure calculations.

claim: Tetrapeptides with a B-φ-B-φ motif (SS-31 and SPN4) had lower root mean square deviation (RMSD) values and three non-sequential NOEs.
source: Specifically, tetrapeptides with a B-φ-B-φ motif (SS-31 and SPN4) had lower root mean square deviation (RMSD) values (better structural precision) and three non-sequential NOEs, whereas those with a φ-B-φ-B motif (SS-20 and SPN10) lacked non-sequential NOEs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Tetrapeptides with a φ-B-φ-B motif (SS-20 and SPN10) lacked non-sequential NOEs.
source: Specifically, tetrapeptides with a B-φ-B-φ motif (SS-31 and SPN4) had lower root mean square deviation (RMSD) values (better structural precision) and three non-sequential NOEs, whereas those with a φ-B-φ-B motif (SS-20 and SPN10) lacked non-sequential NOEs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The non-sequential NOEs in SS-31 and SPN4 occurred between the two aromatic residues.
source: Importantly, the non-sequential NOEs in SS-31 and SPN4 occurred between the two aromatic residues, consistent with previous observations that residual structure is more common in short peptides containing aromatic side chains (Neri et al., 1992; Smith et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Residual structure is more common in short peptides containing aromatic side chains.
source: Importantly, the non-sequential NOEs in SS-31 and SPN4 occurred between the two aromatic residues, consistent with previous observations that residual structure is more common in short peptides containing aromatic side chains (Neri et al., 1992; Smith et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cation-π interactions between neighboring basic and aromatic amino acids stabilize the tetrapeptide structures in solution.
source: Additional interactions that appear to stabilize the tetrapeptide structures in solution are cation-π interactions between neighboring basic and aromatic amino acids.
evidence: This is an inference based on NMR chemical shift data.

claim: Cation-π interactions are supported by significant upfield ring current shifts for some of the basic residue side chain nuclei for all peptides except SS-31.
source: These are supported by significant upfield ring current shifts for some of the basic residue side chain nuclei (Supplementary file 1), for all peptides except SS-31.
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: All-atom MD simulations (200 ns each) of the peptides in an aqueous environment were performed.
source: As a second approach to assessing peptide solution structures, we performed all-atom MD simulations (200 ns each) of the peptides in an aqueous environment.
evidence: This is a description of the computational methods used.

claim: The MD-derived ensembles had greater structural variability (higher RMSD) and were less compact (higher Rg) than their cognate NMR-derived structures.
source: The MD-derived ensembles had greater structural variability (higher RMSD) and were less compact (higher Rg) than their cognate NMR-derived structures (Figure 1C, compare black squares and circles).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of NMR and MD data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The RMSD values calculated by MD simulations were lower for SS-31 and SPN4 than for SS-20 and SPN10.
source: However, consistent with our NMR results, the RMSD values calculated by MD simulations were lower for SS-31 and SPN4 than for SS-20 and SPN10 (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The free peptides are largely disordered but retain some residual structure due to cation-π and aromatic ring stacking interactions.
source: Taken together, the results of our NMR and MD analyses suggest that the free peptides are largely disordered but retain some residual structure due to cation-π and aromatic ring stacking interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR and MD data.

claim: All tetrapeptides bound CL-containing membranes with roughly similar binding affinity (KD 27.5 µM to 39.5 µM; ΔG –26.2 kJ/mol to –25.9 kJ/mol).
source: First, all tetrapeptides bound CL-containing membranes with roughly similar binding affinity (KD 27.5 µM to 39.5 µM; ΔG –26.2 kJ/mol to –25.9 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The binding affinity values did not differ significantly among the analogs.
source: These binding affinity values did not differ significantly among the analogs.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The lipid-to-peptide binding stoichiometry, n, differed among peptides.
source: However, the lipid-to-peptide binding stoichiometry, n, did differ among peptides.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SPN4 had a similar lipid-to-peptide stoichiometry (n=5.7) to SS-31 (n=5.4).
source: Compared with the benchmark SS-31 (n=5.4; i.e. an average of 5.4 lipids per bound peptide), SPN4 had a similar value (n=5.7), SS-20 had a significantly higher value (n=7.4), and SPN10 had a significantly lower value (n=3.3).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SS-20 had a significantly higher lipid-to-peptide stoichiometry (n=7.4) than SS-31 (n=5.4).
source: Compared with the benchmark SS-31 (n=5.4; i.e. an average of 5.4 lipids per bound peptide), SPN4 had a similar value (n=5.7), SS-20 had a significantly higher value (n=7.4), and SPN10 had a significantly lower value (n=3.3).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SPN10 had a significantly lower lipid-to-peptide stoichiometry (n=3.3) than SS-31 (n=5.4).
source: Compared with the benchmark SS-31 (n=5.4; i.e. an average of 5.4 lipids per bound peptide), SPN4 had a similar value (n=5.7), SS-20 had a significantly higher value (n=7.4), and SPN10 had a significantly lower value (n=3.3).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SPN10 and SS-20 bind membranes, respectively, at higher and lower surface densities than SS-31.
source: These results indicate that SPN10 and SS-20 bind membranes, respectively, at higher and lower surface densities than SS-31.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid-to-peptide stoichiometry values from ITC.

claim: Membrane interaction of all peptides was enthalpically favorable (ΔH<0) and entropically favorable (TΔS>0), with binding dominated by entropy.
source: Membrane interaction of all peptides was enthalpically favorable (ΔH<0) and entropically favorable (TΔS>0), with binding dominated by entropy as observed previously for SS-31 (Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SPN4 had a similar binding enthalpy (ΔH=–4.5 kJ/mol) to SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol).
source: In comparison with the binding enthalpy of SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol), SPN4 had a similar value (ΔH=–4.5 kJ/mol), whereas the magnitude of binding enthalpy was significantly lower for SS-20 (ΔH=–3.2 kJ/mol) and higher for SPN10 (ΔH=–7.1 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The magnitude of binding enthalpy was significantly lower for SS-20 (ΔH=–3.2 kJ/mol) than for SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol).
source: In comparison with the binding enthalpy of SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol), SPN4 had a similar value (ΔH=–4.5 kJ/mol), whereas the magnitude of binding enthalpy was significantly lower for SS-20 (ΔH=–3.2 kJ/mol) and higher for SPN10 (ΔH=–7.1 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The magnitude of binding enthalpy was significantly higher for SPN10 (ΔH=–7.1 kJ/mol) than for SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol).
source: In comparison with the binding enthalpy of SS-31 (ΔH=–5.1 kJ/mol), SPN4 had a similar value (ΔH=–4.5 kJ/mol), whereas the magnitude of binding enthalpy was significantly lower for SS-20 (ΔH=–3.2 kJ/mol) and higher for SPN10 (ΔH=–7.1 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The trend in ΔH is consistent with the number of aromatic side chains containing polar groups.
source: As ΔH is a function of polar contacts made during binding (Seelig, 2004), this trend in ΔH is consistent with the number of aromatic side chains containing polar groups (SPN10, two indole NH groups; SPN4/SS-31, one phenol OH group; SS-20, none).
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data and knowledge of peptide chemistry.

claim: Binding entropy did not differ significantly among peptides (TΔS ranged from 19.0 to 22.1 kJ/mol).
source: Binding entropy, which in this system is largely a function of aromatic side chain partitioning into the acyl chain region (Seelig, 2004), did not differ significantly among peptides (TΔS ranged from 19.0 to 22.1 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In comparison with SS-31, membrane binding of SS-20 is more entropy-driven.
source: However, the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions to binding, quantified by the ratio TΔS/|ΔH|, indicate that in comparison with SS-31, membrane binding of SS-20 is more entropy-driven and that of SPN10 is more enthalpy-driven.
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In comparison with SS-31, membrane binding of SPN10 is more enthalpy-driven.
source: However, the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions to binding, quantified by the ratio TΔS/|ΔH|, indicate that in comparison with SS-31, membrane binding of SS-20 is more entropy-driven and that of SPN10 is more enthalpy-driven.
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the presence of CL-containing bicelles, the NMR signals of SS-31 broaden at low peptide:lipid ratios and then sharpen again at a molar excess of peptide to CL.
source: As previously reported (Birk et al., 2014), in the presence of CL-containing bicelles, the NMR signals of SS-31 broaden at low peptide:lipid ratios and then sharpen again at a molar excess of peptide to CL.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The free and bicelle-bound states of the peptides are in fast exchange on the NMR time-scale.
source: This indicates that the free and bicelle-bound states of the peptides are in fast exchange on the NMR time-scale and should be amenable to transferred NOE (trNOE) studies (Post, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on NMR observations and a citation to NMR theory.

claim: The structures of all four peptides bound to bicelles were calculated based on a large number of negative NOEs.
source: The structures of all four peptides bound to bicelles (Figure 3) were calculated based on a large number of negative NOEs, consistent with a high MW peptide-bicelle complex, that are transferred to the free peptide (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panel C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The NMR structures of bound peptides are precise, with heavy atom RMSDs values of 0.5–0.9 Å.
source: The NMR structures are precise because they are each defined by 95–110 trNOEs per tetrapeptide or about 25 structural restraints per residue (Supplementary file 3). This is reflected in heavy atom RMSDs values of 0.5–0.9 Å for the bound peptides, which is less than half of those of the free peptides (compare Figure 1C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data in Supplementary file 3 and Figure 1C.

claim: NMR structures of all the peptide analogs had lower RMSD and Rg values in the membrane-bound relative to the free state.
source: NMR structures of all the peptide analogs had lower RMSD and Rg values in the membrane-bound relative to the free state.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All peptide analogs except SS-31 became more structurally constrained and compact upon binding.
source: In other words, they became more structurally constrained and compact upon binding (Figure 1C, compare black and red squares). The exception was SS-31, whose RMSD and Rg values did not statistically change upon binding.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SS-31's RMSD and Rg values did not statistically change upon binding.
source: In other words, they became more structurally constrained and compact upon binding (Figure 1C, compare black and red squares). The exception was SS-31, whose RMSD and Rg values did not statistically change upon binding.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All peptide analogs except for SS-31 formed H-bonded reverse turn structures in the membrane-bound state.
source: Interestingly, we found that in the membrane-bound state, all peptide analogs except for SS-31 formed H-bonded reverse turn structures with basic side chains pointing away from the plane of the backbone ring (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The reverse turn structures give the peptides a markedly asymmetric charge distribution.
source: This gives the peptides a markedly asymmetric charge distribution (shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with the cationic face of the peptides likely poised for binding to the negatively charged lipid phosphates of CL-containing membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR structures shown in Figure 3 and electrostatic calculations in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The φ-B-φ-B peptides have CO(1) to NH(4) H-bonds to form the reverse turn structures.
source: To form the reverse turn structures, the φ-B-φ-B peptides have CO(1) to NH(4) H-bonds.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the B-φ-B-φ peptide SPN4, the H-bond is formed with the capping NH2 group in a CO(2) to NH2(5) pattern.
source: However, for the B-φ-B-φ peptide SPN4, the H-bond is formed with the capping NH2 group that essentially acts as the amide proton donor of a non-existent fifth residue in a CO(2) to NH2(5) pattern (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SS-31 adopts an extended conformation due to steric restraints induced by the methyl groups on Dmt2 that preclude the turn conformation from forming.
source: In contrast, the other B-φ-B-φ peptide SS-31 adopts an extended conformation due to steric restraints induced by the methyl groups on Dmt2 that preclude the turn conformation from forming.
evidence: This is an inference based on NMR data shown in Figure 3 and knowledge of steric effects.

claim: For the peptides that form a reverse turn, intra-peptide cation-π interactions are observed.
source: For the peptides that form a reverse turn, intra-peptide cation-π interactions are observed, and the backbone H-bond NH donor in the turn structure is always an aromatic residue.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The backbone H-bond NH donor in the turn structure is always an aromatic residue.
source: For the peptides that form a reverse turn, intra-peptide cation-π interactions are observed, and the backbone H-bond NH donor in the turn structure is always an aromatic residue.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All peptides rapidly adsorbed to the membrane surface within 500–750 ns in MD simulations.
source: All peptides rapidly adsorbed to the membrane surface within 500–750 ns and evolved toward a stable, bound configuration over the course of the 2 µs simulations (see Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5.

claim: Membrane-bound structures from MD had higher RMSD and Rg values than those from NMR.
source: As with the solution structures, membrane-bound structures from MD had higher RMSD and Rg values than those from NMR (compare Figure 1C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of NMR and MD data in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The MD ensembles had a low frequency of sampling states with high similarity to the NMR-derived structures.
source: Overall, the MD ensembles had a low frequency of sampling states with high similarity to the NMR-derived structures (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Imposing the NMR restraints yielded considerable improvements in structural similarity to the NMR structure for all peptides.
source: Imposing the NMR restraints yielded considerable improvements in structural similarity to the NMR structure for all peptides (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NOE violations occurred less than 20% of the time for the majority (~71%) of the applied restraints in MD simulations.
source: NOE violations were computed over the MD simulations using time and ensemble averaging and violations occurred less than 20% of the time for the majority (~71%) of the applied restraints (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The residues of SS-31 tended to bury deepest, followed sequentially by SPN10, SS-20, and SPN4.
source: Generally, the residues of SS-31 tended to bury deepest, followed sequentially by SPN10, SS-20, and SPN4.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Most of the peptide-lipid NOEs were from aromatic residues to lipid protons close to the headgroup region.
source: Most of the peptide-lipid NOEs were from aromatic residues to lipid protons close to the headgroup region.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Peptides are superficially buried in the interfacial region of lipid bilayers.
source: This suggests peptides are superficially buried in the interfacial region of lipid bilayers, in agreement with the MD results.
evidence: This is an inference based on NMR and MD data.

claim: The peptide-lipid NOEs for SPN10 were generally weaker than those of the other peptides.
source: Interestingly, the peptide-lipid NOEs for SPN10 were generally weaker than those of the other peptides (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The presence of all peptides at the bilayer interface reduced both lipid headgroup and acyl chain SASA.
source: As expected, the presence of all peptides at the bilayer interface reduced both lipid headgroup and acyl chain SASA, due to peptides 'covering' the bilayer surface.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SS-20 and SPN4 were more solvent exposed than SS-31 and SPN10.
source: Among the four analogs, SS-20 and SPN4 were more solvent exposed, consistent with their more superficial binding near the solvent interface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: SS-31 and SPN10 caused the greatest decrease in acyl chain SASA.
source: By comparison, SS-31 and SPN10 caused the greatest decrease in acyl chain SASA, consistent with their deeper burial into the non-polar core (Figure 4C), filling the 'voids' of solvent-exposed hydrocarbon chains.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: SPN10 caused a significantly lower headgroup SASA than other peptides.
source: The most notable distinction between the more deeply buried SS-31 and SPN10 was that SPN10 also caused a significantly lower headgroup SASA.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SPN10-containing bilayers had the lowest total SASA among all peptide analogs.
source: Hence, SPN10-containing bilayers had the lowest total SASA among all peptide analogs, and SPN10 was the only peptide to not significantly change the total SASA compared to the bilayer-only system.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SPN10 was the only peptide to not significantly change the total SASA compared to the bilayer-only system.
source: Hence, SPN10-containing bilayers had the lowest total SASA among all peptide analogs, and SPN10 was the only peptide to not significantly change the total SASA compared to the bilayer-only system.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SS-31 and SPN10 expanded mean lipid area (decreased bilayer thickness) to a greater extent than did SPN4 and SS-20.
source: SS-31 and SPN10 expanded mean lipid area (decreased bilayer thickness) to a greater extent than did SPN4 and SS-20, which is likely related to the deeper burial of SS-31 and SPN10 aromatic side chains into the membrane (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: SPN10 both expanded membrane area and maintained the lowest total SASA.
source: The combined observations that SPN10 both expanded membrane area (Figure 4—figure supplement 8) and maintained the lowest total SASA (Figure 4D) suggest that even though this analog causes elastic bilayer expansion, it maintains a low 'ruggedness' of exposed membrane surface (Tüchsen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on MD data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: SS-31 and SPN4 had a greater density of CL phosphates in the closest shells around Arg.
source: SS-31 and SPN4 had a greater density of CL phosphates in the closest shells, whereas CL phosphates of distal radial shells were more populated for SS-20 and SPN10.
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: SPN10 disfavored close contact of CL.
source: By comparison, SPN10 disfavored close contact of CL, which may be related to its large aromatic Trp side chains inhibiting close approach of sterically bulky CL.
evidence: This is an inference based on MD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: All peptides caused a saturable decrease in membrane surface charge.
source: All peptides caused a saturable decrease in membrane surface charge, with SPN10 causing markedly higher attenuation (Figure 5A, left); by comparison, within the resolution of this assay, there was no discernible difference in saturation binding among peptides (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is supported by ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SPN10 caused markedly higher attenuation of membrane surface charge than other peptides.
source: All peptides caused a saturable decrease in membrane surface charge, with SPN10 causing markedly higher attenuation (Figure 5A, left); by comparison, within the resolution of this assay, there was no discernible difference in saturation binding among peptides (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is supported by ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SPN10 showed the greatest effect on ψs in a lipid-only system.
source: Again, SPN10 showed the greatest effect on ψs in this lipid-only system (Figure 5B, left) despite all analogs having similar saturation curves (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This is supported by ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SPN10 is a markedly more potent attenuator of membrane surface charge, originating from down-tuning of lipid bilayer surface charge.
source: Taken together, these results show that SPN10 is a markedly more potent attenuator of membrane surface charge, originating from down-tuning of lipid bilayer surface charge.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: All peptides caused saturable reduction in ψd.
source: Titration of LUVs with peptides resulted in a saturable reduction in ψd (Figure 5C, left) with fractional binding (Figure 5C, right) consistent with our ITC-based binding curves (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by di-8-ANEPPS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All peptides cause saturable disordering of lipid and/or water dipoles upon binding.
source: These results indicate that all peptides cause saturable disordering of lipid and/or water dipoles upon binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on di-8-ANEPPS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SS-20 had a markedly weaker effect on ψd than the others.
source: Furthermore, SS-20 had a markedly weaker effect than the others, possibly due to its comparatively lower aromatic bulk and/or lack of polar groups on aromatic side chains.
evidence: This is an inference based on di-8-ANEPPS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No peptides had any measurable effect on the TMRM-detected magnitude of ΔΨm.
source: No peptides had any measurable effect on the TMRM-detected magnitude of ΔΨm (Figure 5D), indicating that they neither hyperpolarize nor depolarize the IMM under the conditions tested.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The peptides neither hyperpolarize nor depolarize the IMM under the conditions tested.
source: No peptides had any measurable effect on the TMRM-detected magnitude of ΔΨm (Figure 5D), indicating that they neither hyperpolarize nor depolarize the IMM under the conditions tested.
evidence: This is an inference based on TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The two biotinylated peptides readily penetrated both cell lines within an hour and showed a mitochondrial localization pattern.
source: The two biotinylated peptides readily penetrated both cell lines within an hour and showed a mitochondrial localization pattern (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell uptake and mitochondrial localization are supported by either of the two possible sequence registers for these tetrapeptides.
source: These results indicate that cell uptake and mitochondrial localization are supported by either of the two possible sequence registers for these tetrapeptides.
evidence: This is an inference based on cell culture data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells grown in the absence of serum for 3 days showed a clear mitochondrial depolarization relative to positive controls grown with serum.
source: Cells grown in the absence of serum for 3 days showed a clear mitochondrial depolarization relative to positive controls grown with serum (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Three peptides showed partial restoration of ΔΨm within 2 hr of treatment.
source: Interestingly, three peptides showed partial restoration of ΔΨm on a remarkably short timescale, within 2 hr of treatment.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SS-31 caused a significant increase in TMRM signal (p<0.05) following treatment of serum-deprived cell culture with 10 nM peptide.
source: Following the treatment of serum-deprived cell culture with 10 nM peptide, the benchmark SS-31 caused a significant increase in TMRM signal (p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The TMRM signal of SPN4-treated cells was not significantly higher than serum-deprived cells.
source: By comparison, the TMRM signal of SPN4-treated cells was not significantly higher than serum-deprived cells, whereas that of cells treated with SS-20 (p<0.01) and SPN10 (p<0.001) was significantly higher than those treated with SS-31.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The TMRM signal of cells treated with SS-20 (p<0.01) and SPN10 (p<0.001) was significantly higher than those treated with SS-31.
source: By comparison, the TMRM signal of SPN4-treated cells was not significantly higher than serum-deprived cells, whereas that of cells treated with SS-20 (p<0.01) and SPN10 (p<0.001) was significantly higher than those treated with SS-31.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cells grown in the absence of serum showed fragmentation of the mitochondrial reticular network with perinuclear clustering in comparison with the extended network observed with non-stressed cells in the presence of serum.
source: Cells grown in the absence of serum showed fragmentation of the mitochondrial reticular network with perinuclear clustering in comparison with the extended network observed with non-stressed cells in the presence of serum.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with any of the four peptides for 2 hr before observation resulted in restoration of the reticular network pattern seen in the absence of stress.
source: Consistent with the rapid kinetics observed for TMRM measurements, treatment with any of the four peptides for 2 hr before observation resulted in restoration of the reticular network pattern seen in the absence of stress.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mode of action of these peptides entails a rapid repolarization of the IMM and restoration of the mitochondrial network when challenged with serum withdrawal stress.
source: Taken together, these results strongly support that the mode of action of these peptides entails a rapid repolarization of the IMM and restoration of the mitochondrial network when challenged with serum withdrawal stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cell culture data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When grown with serum-containing media for 3 days, the presence of peptide had no effect on viability.
source: Control tests confirmed that when grown with serum-containing media for 3 days, the presence of peptide had no effect on viability (Figure 6C, left), consistent with previous observations that SS-31 has no effect under non-stressed conditions (Szeto, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When cells were subject to serum deprivation conditions for 7 days, the presence of peptide strongly improved cell survival.
source: However, when cells were subject to serum deprivation conditions for 7 days, the presence of peptide strongly improved cell survival (Figure 6C, right); in this case, we observed marked differences in potency among the peptides, with SPN10 significantly outperforming SS-31 (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SPN10 significantly outperformed SS-31 (p<0.001) in promoting cell survival under serum deprivation.
source: However, when cells were subject to serum deprivation conditions for 7 days, the presence of peptide strongly improved cell survival (Figure 6C, right); in this case, we observed marked differences in potency among the peptides, with SPN10 significantly outperforming SS-31 (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Peptides show the same trends in cellular ATP as in cell viability with SPN10 significantly better than SS-31 (p<0.001).
source: We observed a striking parallel with the results from our viability tests, wherein peptides show the same trends in cellular ATP with SPN10 significantly better than SS-31 (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SPN10 significantly raised ATP levels in ARPE-19 cells with serum starvation.
source: In addition, SPN10 significantly raised ATP levels in ARPE-19 cells with serum starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, panel B).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under the serum-free conditions tested, all four peptide analogs displayed mitochondrial protection to varying degrees.
source: Taken together, our cell culture studies show that, under the serum-free conditions tested, all four peptide analogs displayed mitochondrial protection to varying degrees.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SPN4<SS-31<SS-20<SPN10 for ΔΨm restoration.
source: Based on our quantified cell culture measurements, the rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SPN4<SS-31<SS-20<SPN10 for ΔΨm restoration, SS-31=SS-20<SPN4<SPN10 for cell viability, and SS-31<SS-20=SPN4<SPN10 for cellular ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SS-31=SS-20<SPN4<SPN10 for cell viability.
source: Based on our quantified cell culture measurements, the rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SPN4<SS-31<SS-20<SPN10 for ΔΨm restoration, SS-31=SS-20<SPN4<SPN10 for cell viability, and SS-31<SS-20=SPN4<SPN10 for cellular ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SS-31<SS-20=SPN4<SPN10 for cellular ATP.
source: Based on our quantified cell culture measurements, the rank order of peptide analog effectiveness was SPN4<SS-31<SS-20<SPN10 for ΔΨm restoration, SS-31=SS-20<SPN4<SPN10 for cell viability, and SS-31<SS-20=SPN4<SPN10 for cellular ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of cell culture data shown in Figure 6.

claim: All four analogs were found to bind CL-containing bilayers, modulate membrane electrostatics, and show mitochondrial protection in cell stress models.
source: All four analogs were found to bind CL-containing bilayers, modulate membrane electrostatics, and show mitochondrial protection in cell stress models.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The general motif of alternating cationic and aromatic residues is sufficient for the molecular action of these mitochondria-targeted compounds.
source: Collectively, these observations support the concept that this general motif is sufficient for the molecular action of these mitochondria-targeted compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that all four analogs showed activity.

claim: All peptides are largely disordered in solution and assumed a more compact and well-defined structure when membrane-bound.
source: As expected, all peptides are largely disordered in solution (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–) and assumed a more compact and well-defined structure when membrane-bound (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Intra-peptide aromatic ring stacking and cation-π interactions are stabilizing features of both the solution and membrane-bound states.
source: Intra-peptide aromatic ring stacking and cation-π interactions are stabilizing features of both the solution and membrane-bound states (Figure 1B and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Cation-π complexes lower the energetic cost of partitioning basic side chains into the non-polar membrane core.
source: This point is significant because cation-π complexes are known to lower the energetic cost of partitioning basic side chains into the non-polar membrane core (Hohlweg et al., 2018; Infield et al., 2021), which likely contributes to the ability of these tetrapeptide analogs to traverse cell membranes, including those of the blood-brain barrier (Zhao et al., 2003; Reddy et al., 2017), and to reside stably at the membrane interface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The membrane-bound reverse-turn conformation is the most notable structural feature of these tetrapeptides.
source: The most notable structural feature of these tetrapeptides is the membrane-bound reverse-turn conformation observed for all analogs other than SS-31.
evidence: This is a summary of the NMR structural findings.

claim: These conformers can all be formally classified as four-residue beta turns stabilized by an i to i+3 main chain H-bond with an Cα(1) to Cα(4) distance of ~7 Å or less.
source: These conformers can all be formally classified as four-residue beta turns stabilized by an i to i+3 main chain H-bond with an Cα(1) to Cα(4) distance of ~7 Å or less (Venkatachalam, 1968; Lewis et al., 1973).
evidence: This is a classification based on NMR structures and citations to structural definitions.

claim: C-terminal amidation provides an H-bond donor to stabilize the turn structure of peptides with B-φ-B-φ register.
source: This latter feature underscores the importance of C-terminal amidation in these compounds: not only does the amide remove the C-terminal carboxyl function to maintain the net +3 charge of these compounds, but as shown in this study, it also provides an H-bond donor to stabilize the turn structure of peptides with B-φ-B-φ register.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR structure of SPN4.

claim: The i to i+3 polar interaction partially offsets the energetic penalty of dehydration of polar backbone functional groups at the membrane.
source: By partially satisfying the H-bonding capacity of main chain atoms, this i to i+3 polar interaction partially offsets the energetic penalty of dehydration of polar backbone functional groups at the membrane, which may in turn allow the peptides to reside near the polar-apolar boundary of the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR structures and knowledge of membrane biophysics.

claim: SPN10 has a greater binding density than SS-31/SPN4.
source: Hence, SPN10 has a greater binding density, and SS-20 has a lower binding density compared with SS-31/SPN4.
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data and lipid area calculations.

claim: SS-20 has a lower binding density compared with SS-31/SPN4.
source: Hence, SPN10 has a greater binding density, and SS-20 has a lower binding density compared with SS-31/SPN4.
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data and lipid area calculations.

claim: The greater per-peptide membrane coverage of SPN10 may relate to its enhanced efficacy by increased occupancy of the limited lipid area of mitochondria.
source: Given that the mitochondrial IMM is protein-rich with little free exposed bilayer (Capaldi, 1982), the greater per-peptide membrane coverage of SPN10 may relate to its enhanced efficacy by increased occupancy of the limited lipid area of mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculation based on ITC data and knowledge of mitochondrial membrane composition.

claim: SPN10 stood apart from the other peptides in that it minimized solvent exposure of both lipid aliphatic chains and headgroups.
source: In the present study, we found that SPN10 stood apart from the other peptides in that it minimized solvent exposure of both lipid aliphatic chains and headgroups, thereby resulting in total membrane SASA similar to membranes in the absence of peptide (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by MD data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ability of SPN10 to fill packing defects is likely related to a combination of factors, including its large aromatic side chain volume, its deeper binding in the membrane interface, and its high surface coverage.
source: This ability of SPN10 to fill packing defects is likely related to a combination of factors, including its large aromatic side chain volume, its deeper binding in the membrane interface (Figure 4C), and its high surface coverage (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on MD and ITC data.

claim: Reducing lipid packing voids could be part of the mechanism of action of these tetrapeptides.
source: Reducing lipid packing voids could be part of the MoA of these tetrapeptides, contributing to the observed decrease in proton leak across the IMM (Zhang et al., 2020) and lipid oxidative damage (Zhao et al., 2005; Min et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017) that occurs with SS-31 treatment.
evidence: This is speculation based on MD data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Bound peptides reside in the membrane interface, likely within the boundaries of the lipid phosphate and ester groups.
source: Our trNOE (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and MD (Figure 4C) results both indicate that bound peptides reside in the membrane interface, likely within the boundaries of the lipid phosphate and ester groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR and MD data.

claim: All analogs had roughly equal KD (ΔG) values, with binding dominated by favorable changes in entropy.
source: All analogs had roughly equal KD (ΔG) values, with binding dominated by favorable changes in entropy (mean TΔS/|ΔH| ranged from 2.7 to 6.9).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The large and favorable binding entropy originates largely from the classical hydrophobic effect: membrane penetration of aromatic side chains is attendant with increased solvent mobility that accompanies the desolvation of the peptide and the release of ordered waters from non-polar acyl surfaces.
source: Instead, the large and favorable binding entropy we observe originates largely from the classical hydrophobic effect: membrane penetration of aromatic side chains is attendant with increased solvent mobility that accompanies the desolvation of the peptide and the release of ordered waters from non-polar acyl surfaces (Seelig, 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on ITC data and a citation to thermodynamic theory.

claim: Membrane binding of SS-20 is dominated by entropically favored burial of its aromatic Phe side chains in the non-polar membrane core.
source: We propose that membrane binding of SS-20 is dominated by entropically favored burial of its aromatic Phe side chains, which lack polar groups, in the non-polar membrane core.
evidence: This is speculation based on ITC data and knowledge of peptide chemistry.

claim: Membrane binding of SPN10 is strongly favored by polar interactions involving the indole NH hydrogen bond donors of its Trp side chains.
source: By comparison, binding enthalpy originates largely from polar interactions between peptide and lipid headgroups. We propose that membrane binding of SPN10 is strongly favored by polar interactions involving the indole NH hydrogen bond donors of its Trp side chains.
evidence: This is speculation based on ITC data and knowledge of peptide chemistry.

claim: The interaction of these peptides with membranes shows enthalpy-entropy compensation.
source: Finally, our analysis suggests that the interaction of these peptides with membranes shows enthalpy-entropy compensation, wherein the binding energy of a congeneric series of compounds remains relatively constant due to opposing changes in ΔH and ΔS (Fox et al., 2018), as observed with the surface interactions of different peptides (Wang et al., 2020; Meier and Seelig, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data and citations to thermodynamic theory.

claim: The ψs of negatively-charged membranes was attenuated by all peptides.
source: First, the ψs of negatively-charged membranes (biomimetic liposomes and mitoplasts) was attenuated by all peptides (Figure 5A and B); however, SPN10 had the greatest effect by far.
evidence: This is supported by ANS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The ψd of bilayers was down-regulated by all peptides.
source: Second, the ψd of bilayers, related to the ordering of lipid polar groups and interfacial waters, was down-regulated by all peptides (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by di-8-ANEPPS fluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No peptide affected the ΔΨm, supporting that they do not depolarize or hyperpolarize mitochondrial membrane potentials.
source: Finally, it is notable that no peptide affected the ΔΨm (Figure 5D), supporting that they do not depolarize or hyperpolarize mitochondrial membrane potentials, consistent with the strong safety profile of SS-31 and SS-20.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The tuning of ψs is an important part of the mechanism of action of these peptides.
source: Our working model posits that the tuning of ψs is an important part of the MoA of these peptides, potentially by modulating interactions of cations and polybasic proteins with CL-containing membranes or facilitating curvature by lowering headgroup anionic repulsion (Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects on ψs and a citation to prior work.

claim: Both biotinylated variants of SS-31 and SPN10 accumulated in the mitochondrial network when added to two different types of human endothelial cells.
source: On one hand, the peptides showed many functional similarities in mammalian cell lines: (i) both biotinylated variants of SS-31 and SPN10 accumulated in the mitochondrial network when added to two different types of human endothelial cells (Figure 6A), indicating that cell permeation and mitochondria targeting are sequence-promiscuous, without strict requirement for a specific side chain register or identity of aromatic side chains
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell permeation and mitochondria targeting are sequence-promiscuous, without strict requirement for a specific side chain register or identity of aromatic side chains.
